---
title: "Quiz: sparsity and the ℓ1 penalty"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Conventions as in the lecture: ℓ1 penalty λ|x|, ℓ2 penalty (λ/2)x², ℓ0 a fixed cost per nonzero.

---

**Q1.** What is the difference between a **sparse** and a **compressible** signal? Give an example of each.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Sort the coefficients by size.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sparse: only $K$ coefficients are nonzero, the rest exactly 0 (eight spikes in the pixel basis, a piecewise-constant signal in the Haar basis). Compressible: no exact zeros, but the sorted magnitudes fall fast, like a power law, so keeping the $K$ largest gives a small error (a real image in a wavelet basis).
:::

---

**Q2.** A signal is a sum of three cosines of different frequencies. In which basis is it sparse: pixels, DCT or Haar? Which signal would be sparse in the Haar basis but not in the DCT?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each basis is made of one kind of shape.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In the DCT (or Fourier) basis: a few coefficients, one or two per cosine. A piecewise-constant signal (a few steps) is sparse in Haar, whose atoms are little steps; in the DCT a step needs many cosines (the ringing of a truncated Fourier series).
:::

---

**Q3.** Shrink $w = (5,\ -2,\ 0.7,\ -0.2)$ with λ = 1.5: (a) with the ℓ1 penalty (soft threshold), (b) with the ℓ2 penalty. How many zeros does each give?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
ℓ1: subtract 1.5 from each magnitude, stop at 0. ℓ2: divide by 1 + λ.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) (3.5, −0.5, 0, 0): two zeros. (b) $w/2.5$ = (2, −0.8, 0.28, −0.08): no zeros, although the last two are small.
:::

---

**Q4.** In the two-coefficient picture, why does the ℓ1 solution so often lie on an axis, while the ℓ2 solution almost never does?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where does a growing ellipse first touch a diamond? A circle?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The answer is where the smallest misfit ellipse touches the penalty ball. The ℓ1 ball is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes; an ellipse coming from outside most often touches it first at a corner, where one coordinate is exactly 0. The ℓ2 ball is round, with no special points: the touching point can be anywhere and lies on an axis only by coincidence.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why don't we simply minimise the number of nonzeros (ℓ0) directly?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many supports are there with 8 nonzeros among 256 unknowns?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With a general matrix the only exact way is to try supports, and there are about $4 \cdot 10^{14}$ of them for 8 out of 256: a combinatorial search. The ℓ0 penalty is not convex (many valleys). ℓ1 is convex, so simple iterations find the global minimum, and it is the closest convex stand-in for the count.
:::

---

**Q6.** What is λ_max, and what happens to the lasso solution as λ is lowered from λ_max to 0?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
λ_max is the largest correlation of a column with the data.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
λ_max = $\max_j|\mathbf a_j^\top\mathbf y|$: for λ ≥ λ_max all coefficients are exactly 0. As λ falls, coefficients become nonzero one (or a few) at a time, in the order of how strongly their column explains the remaining residual; at λ → 0 we approach the least-squares solution (if it is unique).
:::

---

**Q7.** An ℓ1 reconstruction finds all the right spikes, but each is too low by about the same amount. Why, and how can you fix it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the soft threshold do to coefficients above the threshold?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Shrinkage bias: ℓ1 subtracts about λ from every surviving coefficient (exactly λ in an orthonormal basis). Fix: keep the support that ℓ1 found and refit those coefficients by least squares (debiasing), or use reweighted ℓ1.
:::

---

**Q8.** Which prior on the coefficients corresponds to the ℓ1 penalty, and why does it fit wavelet coefficients of images better than a Gaussian?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at the histogram of wavelet details on a log scale.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The Laplace prior, $p(c) \propto e^{-|c|/b}$. Wavelet details of images are sharply peaked at 0 (smooth regions) with heavy tails (edges): on a log scale the histogram has straight-line tails, like the Laplace density. A Gaussian with the same spread falls off far too quickly and makes the large edge coefficients almost impossible.
:::

---

**Q9.** Total variation is "ℓ1 of the differences". Why does it keep a step but turn a ramp into a staircase?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Count the nonzero differences of a step and of a ramp.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A step has one nonzero difference, so it is sparse in differences and costs little. A ramp has many small nonzero differences; ℓ1 prefers to set many of them to 0 and concentrate the change in a few larger jumps: a staircase. This is analysis sparsity (a transform of the image is sparse), as opposed to synthesis sparsity (the image is a few atoms).
:::

---

**Q10.** *(math)* Show that the ℓ0 problem $\min_c \tfrac12(c - w)^2 + μ[c \ne 0]$ is solved by a hard threshold, and find the threshold.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the two candidates $c = 0$ and $c = w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If $c \ne 0$ the best is $c = w$ with cost μ; if $c = 0$ the cost is $\tfrac12 w^2$. Keep $w$ iff $\tfrac12 w^2 > μ$, i.e. $|w| > \sqrt{2μ}$: a hard threshold at $\sqrt{2μ}$ (= λ for μ = λ²/2).
:::
